transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I guess they wanted me to come in because of something that happened at work. I’m an EMT, and at the station I was… organizing some airway bags. It probably looked strange, but I was trying to get them in the right pattern.

I was saying some dispatch numbers out loud, kind of repeating them, and my lieutenant told me to stop and step away. I didn’t really… do that right away. It felt important to finish the sequence, like if I broke it, the whole bay would be wrong or go bad somehow.

I know that probably doesn’t sound great. I’m not trying to cause problems. They just thought I should talk to someone.
When you were trying to finish that pattern, did it feel like something you had to do to relieve a strong anxiety or tension?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t say I was panicking exactly. It just felt really wrong to stop. Like there was this pressure that the bags had to be in the right pattern, and the dispatch numbers had to line up in my head.

When my lieutenant told me to step away, I knew I probably should, but it felt like if I broke the sequence the whole bay would… I don’t know, go bad somehow. I know that sounds odd. I was just trying to finish it so things felt right.
At the time, did you believe the bay really would go bad if you stopped, or did it feel more like a thought that didn’t fully make sense but was hard to ignore?

I mean… I know how it sounds, so I don’t want to say it the wrong way. It wasn’t just like a random silly thought, exactly.

At the station, there’s already been… stuff going on, like the injury review people and some supervisors watching me through the cameras, and I’m pretty sure some of my triage notes have been changed so I look unsafe. They say it’s just routine paperwork, and I try to accept that, but it doesn’t feel routine to me.

So when the bay felt wrong, it felt connected to that, like if I didn’t finish it, it would be used against me somehow. I’m not trying to be difficult. I know that may sound paranoid or whatever, but that’s how it felt at the time.
Do you believe for sure that your supervisors are changing your notes and watching you through the cameras?

I… I don’t want to sound like I’m accusing people just to accuse them. I know that wouldn’t be fair.

But yes, I do believe it. The injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras, and I’m pretty sure they’ve been changing my triage notes so it looks like I’m unsafe. They keep saying it’s routine paperwork or normal review, and I try to tell myself maybe that’s all it is, but… it doesn’t feel that way. It feels deliberate.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, anyway. I haven’t, like, seen someone standing there who wasn’t there, or heard a voice talking to me when nobody was around.

Sometimes I get really keyed in on sounds at the station, or I’ll wonder if people are talking about me, but I wouldn’t want to call that hearing things. I mean… if that’s okay to say. I’m not trying to hide anything, I just don’t think I’ve noticed that.
About how long have you believed that your supervisors were watching you through the cameras and changing your notes?

Um… I think it’s been about two months. Maybe a little hard to pin down exactly, but the camera and paperwork stuff has felt like it’s been going on for around the last couple months.

I didn’t really want to make a big deal out of it at first, and I tried to tell myself it was just normal station stuff, but… yeah, around two months is probably fair.
During these past two months, have you had a period where you felt unusually high, energized, or needed much less sleep than usual?

I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had times where I was stressed and maybe running on less sleep than I should, but not like… unusually high or unstoppable or anything.

I haven’t noticed a period where I felt really energized in a good way or didn’t need sleep. If anything, I’d say I’ve just been tense. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
When you feel the need to arrange the bags or repeat the numbers, does that feel like your own mind getting stuck on something you know doesn’t really make sense?

Yeah… I think that’s close. I mean, I know it probably sounds strange, and I’m not trying to make it sound worse than it is.

At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern that felt… right. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Part of me knew it didn’t really make sense, like there wasn’t a normal reason I had to do it, but if I stopped or stepped away, it felt like the whole bay would go bad somehow.

My lieutenant told me to stop and I just… couldn’t step away right then. That’s why they sent me here, I guess. I know that doesn’t sound great.
Did your concerns about being watched and your urge to arrange the bags and repeat the numbers start at about the same time?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, it all kind of blurs together a little, but the camera and paperwork concerns and the stuff at the station with the bags and the numbers were all around the same stretch of time.

I’d say it’s been about the last two months. I don’t know if it was exactly the same day or anything, but it was close enough that… yeah, around the same time.
During these past two months, have you had a period where you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I wouldn’t say depressed most of the day, nearly every day. Not like that, I don’t think.

I’ve been worn down and kind of embarrassed about all this, sure, but I don’t want to overstate it. I still get up and try to do what I’m supposed to do. So… no, I haven’t noticed a steady depressed mood like you’re describing. Is that the right way to answer?
Have these problems been going on for longer than three months?

Yeah… I guess it has been longer than three months, if I’m being accurate.

It really started after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during that ambulance transfer… that was about eight months ago. I didn’t want to make a big thing of it, but that’s when things started feeling off. Does that answer what you mean?
For at least three months, have you believed that your supervisors were watching you through the cameras and changing your notes?

Yeah… for at least three months, yes.

I don’t want to sound like I’m making accusations, but I’ve been pretty sure the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. And the notes… my triage notes haven’t felt right, like they’re being changed or adjusted to make me look unsafe.

They keep saying it’s routine paperwork, and I try to accept that, but it doesn’t feel routine to me. Is that… is that the kind of thing you’re asking?
When you feel you have to arrange the bags or repeat the numbers, do you believe that is actually necessary, or do you feel it doesn’t really make sense even though you can’t resist it?

I mean… part of me knows it probably doesn’t make sense the way it sounds.

But when I’m in it, it feels necessary. Like with the airway bags, I kept moving them into this pattern that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, and I couldn’t really step away even when my lieutenant told me to stop. I wasn’t trying to be difficult. It just felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad somehow.

I know that probably sounds strange. I’m not saying it was logical exactly… it just felt like I had to finish it. Is that what you mean?
Have you ever felt the need to arrange things in patterns or repeat numbers at times when you were not worried about your supervisors watching you or changing your notes?

Um… yeah, I think so. Not always because of the camera thing or the notes.

Like, the reason they sent me here was more about what happened at the station. I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern that just felt… right, I guess. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, and I know I should’ve just listened, but I couldn’t make myself do it right then.

It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad somehow. I know that probably doesn’t sound reasonable. I’m not trying to make excuses—I’m just trying to answer it the right way.
When you have the urge to arrange things or repeat numbers, do you recognize that the fear behind it is probably not really true?

I… I guess I can recognize it later, or part of me can. Like, sitting here, I know saying the whole bay would “go bad” if I didn’t finish the pattern doesn’t sound real.

But at the station, when I was moving the airway bags and repeating the dispatch numbers, it didn’t feel optional. It felt like there was a right way it had to be, and if I broke the sequence something would go wrong. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, and I really didn’t mean to ignore him… I just couldn’t make myself stop right then.

I know that probably isn’t the answer I’m supposed to give. I do understand it sounds unreasonable. It just feels very true when I’m in the middle of it.
When you arrange things or repeat numbers, does that happen even at times when you are not thinking about your supervisors or the cameras?

Yeah… I think it does happen even when I’m not really thinking about them.

I mean, with the airway bags at the station, it wasn’t exactly about supervisors or cameras in that moment. I just kept moving them into this pattern that I knew was right, or felt right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, and I know I should’ve, but I couldn’t really do it right then.

It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. I know that sounds… not reasonable. I’m not trying to make it bigger than it was. That’s just what it felt like at the time.
If someone showed you clear proof that your supervisors were not changing your notes, would you believe it?

I’d want to believe it. I mean, if you showed me something clear, I’d try to take it seriously.

But… honestly, I don’t know if it would fully settle it for me. Because part of me still feels like the injury review people and some supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras and changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe. Even when they say it’s just routine paperwork, it doesn’t feel that way to me.

I know that probably sounds like I’m being difficult. I’m not trying to argue with you. I just… I’m not sure proof would make that feeling go away right away.
Besides the concerns about your supervisors changing your notes and watching you, have you had any other beliefs that other people said were definitely not true?

Not really… I mean, not besides that. At least not that I can think of right now.

The main thing people keep telling me isn’t true is the stuff with the injury review people and some supervisors—like them watching me through the station cameras, and changing my triage notes so it looks like I’m unsafe. They say it’s just routine paperwork, and I understand that’s what I’m supposed to accept.

I don’t want to sound paranoid or like I’m accusing everybody. It’s just… that’s the belief I keep coming back to. I can’t seem to shake it, even when people tell me it’s definitely not happening.
Do you believe your supervisors can change your triage notes by ordinary means, or do you think they are doing it in some impossible or supernatural way?

I don’t think it’s supernatural or anything like that. Not impossible, I guess.

I mean… to me it seems like something they could do through the normal system, like paperwork or computer access, or the review process. The injury review people and some supervisors have access to things, so… that’s where my mind goes.

I know they keep telling me it’s just routine paperwork, and maybe that’s what you’d expect me to say. I’m not trying to make it sound crazy. It just feels like they’re watching me through the station cameras and changing the triage notes in a way that makes me look unsafe.
When the urge to arrange things or repeat numbers comes up, do you try to resist it?

I try to, yeah… or I tell myself I’m trying to. I know it probably looked like I wasn’t listening.

At the station, when I was moving the airway bags into the pattern, it just felt like there was a right way they had to be. And with the dispatch numbers, I kept saying them out loud because stopping felt… wrong. Like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad somehow.

My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, and I should have. I know that. I just couldn’t make myself do it right then. I’m not trying to be difficult or unsafe. It just felt really hard to resist in the moment.
